Draft:

Rivers are among the most patient sculptors of the landscape. As water gathers and flows downhill, it carries sediment, sand, and gravel, grinding against bedrock and loosening soil. Over long spans of time this erosion cuts a channel, and the channel deepens and widens into a valley. In their youth, rivers often carve steep, narrow V-shaped gorges, especially where the land is uplifted or resistant rock slows the cutting. As gradients flatten, streams begin to meander, eroding the outer bank of each bend while depositing sediment on the inner bank, gradually broadening the valley floor. Tributaries join the main stem, extending the drainage network and smoothing hillsides into slopes. Floods periodically spread fertile silt across the floodplain, building flat, rich ground. Glaciers, rainfall, and the underlying rock all modify the pace, but the river remains the central force, endlessly adjusting its course and shaping the terrain we see today.
